chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, who said:
I asked him about two men who stood and looked at the dawn; one of them said, 'It is there,' and the other said, 'I do not see anything.'
He said, 'Let the one for whom dawn has not become clear eat, and eating has become prohibited for the one who claimed that he had seen the dawn.'
Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, says: 'Eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread [of night]. Then complete the fast until the night.'

key_terms.اللَّيْلِ: The night, marking the end of the fasting period at sunset.
key_terms.الْخَيْطُ الْأَبْيَضُ مِنَ الْخَيْطِ الْ: The white thread from the black thread, a metaphorical reference to the distinction between light and darkness at dawn.
key_terms.الْفَجْرُ: Dawn, specifically the time for the Fajr prayer, marking the start of the fasting period.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating when one is unsure if dawn has broken during Ramadan?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) by prioritizing the state of certainty (still in night) over doubt, allowing the uncertain individual to continue eating. It highlights the practical application of Quran 2:187, where the threshold for fasting is defined by objective clarity (*tabayyun*) rather than subjective perception, ensuring that one does not prematurely end the night's sustenance. This ruling underscores the importance of caution in religious obligations while avoiding undue hardship in cases of genuine uncertainty.
